facts.text: On this date in 1587, Virginia Dare became the first English child born in the Americas — in a colony that vanished so completely that its fate remains unsolved 439 years later.
On August 18, 1920, the 19th Amendment was ratified, giving American women the vote — but only after Tennessee's deciding vote was cast by a 24-year-old legislator swayed by a note from his mother.
Monaco is so densely populated that if the entire world lived at the same density, all 8 billion humans would fit inside an area the size of Rhode Island.
The Philippines has more islands than any other country — 7,641 at low tide — yet over half its population lives on just two of them.
Istanbul is the only city on Earth that spans two continents, and each day roughly 1 million people cross between Europe and Asia by commuter ferry alone.
On this date in 1913, the Caisse d'Épargne de Paris paid out its first dividends — over a century before 'democratizing finance' became a Silicon Valley pitch.
On August 18, 1987, the Dow closed above 2,700 for the first time. Eight weeks later it lost 22% in a single day.
The entire US Treasury bond market — roughly $27 trillion — reprices every business day. The global GDP does not.
Berkshire Hathaway's Class A share has never been split. One share costs more than most Americans earn in a decade.
The Dutch East India Company paid an 18% annual dividend for nearly 200 years, funded partly by what today would be classified as war crimes.
On this date in 1868, Pierre Janssen discovered helium in the sun's spectrum during a solar eclipse — 27 years before anyone found it on Earth.
On this date in 1977, Voyager 2 launched. It is now the only human-made object confirmed to have exited the heliosphere alongside its twin.
Your bones are not static scaffolding. The entire adult skeleton replaces itself roughly every decade through a process called remodeling.
A neutron star packs more mass than the sun into a sphere roughly 20 kilometers across. A teaspoon of its material would weigh about a billion tons.
Tardigrades can survive in the vacuum of open space, tolerating radiation doses 1,000 times lethal to humans by entering a state called cryptobiosis.
On this day in 1587, Virginia Dare became the first English child born in the Americas — 20 years before Jamestown existed, and her entire colony vanished without a trace.

On this day in 1920, the 19th Amendment was certified, giving American women the vote. It passed by a single state: Tennessee, decided by a single legislator who changed his mind after his mother wrote him a letter.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — 26 years before the transcontinental railroad was completed. People could transmit documents before they could cross the continent.
Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire. Teaching began at Oxford around 1096; the Aztecs founded Tenochtitlán in 1325.
Woolly mammoths were still alive on Wrangel Island when the Great Pyramid at Giza was already 1,000 years old. Extinction and antiquity are never where we place them.

Sonder (n.): the realization that each passerby has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012. Now it spreads because the feeling always existed; the word did not.
Hiraeth (n.): a Welsh longing for a home that may never have existed — grief, nostalgia, and yearning fused into one untranslatable ache. English requires a sentence; Welsh requires a single breath.

On this day in 1868, French astronomer Pierre Janssen detected a new spectral line in the sun's chromosphere. The element had no name. He called it helium — from Helios, the sun god — decades before it was found on Earth.

Vellichor (n.): the strange wistfulness of used bookshops, where time pools around other people's marginalia. Also a Koenig coinage, proving that naming a feeling can make millions of strangers feel suddenly less alone.

On this day in 1920, the 19th Amendment was certified, giving American women the vote. The word suffrage descends from Latin suffragium — a broken tile used as a ballot in Rome. The shard became a right.
On this day in 2008, Satoshi Nakamoto registered bitcoin.org — two months before publishing the whitepaper. The domain predates the protocol's public existence by 67 days.
On this day in 2020, Ethereum's Beacon Chain genesis deposit contract launched, locking ETH that wouldn't be unlocked for nearly two years until the Merge.
Bitcoin's smallest unit, the satoshi, wasn't named by Satoshi. The term was proposed by Ribuck on the BitcoinTalk forum in November 2010 and adopted by community consensus.
The DAO hack in 2016 didn't exploit a bug in Ethereum — it exploited perfectly valid Solidity. The code did exactly what it said; the specification was the flaw.
Ethereum's EIP-1559, which permanently burns a portion of every transaction fee, has destroyed over 4.3 million ETH since August 2021 — removing it from circulating supply forever.
On this date in 2012, Alex Krizhevsky submitted AlexNet to ImageNet. It cut the error rate by 10 percentage points — a gap so large the computer vision field essentially rerouted overnight.
On August 18, 2020, GPT-3's API opened to the public. OpenAI had trained it on roughly 45TB of text and 175B parameters; most researchers assumed such scale was still years away.

Transformers spend the majority of their compute during inference on matrix multiplications that could, in principle, run on hardware from the 1980s. The architecture is algorithmically old; only the silicon caught up.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known protein universe — in roughly 12 months. The same work would have taken structural biology centuries at prior experimental rates.
Modern LLMs can solve competition-level math problems yet reliably fail at counting the letters in a word. The capability profile is not a point on a scale; it is a strange, uneven surface.
